newsitem.title: NEPAL: NEPAL, INDIA SET TO REVIEW PIVOTAL 1950 TREATY.
newsitem.headline: NEPAL, INDIA SET TO REVIEW PIVOTAL 1950 TREATY.

text.p: Senior diplomats from Nepal and India will meet on August 19 to review a 47-year-old treaty that governs ties between the two South Asian neighbours, the Nepalese foreign minister said on Thursday.

"Nepal and India will hold a foreign secretary level meeting on August 19, 1997, in New Delhi to review the 1950 Nepal India Peace and Friendship Treaty as per the understanding reached between the two countries," state radio quoted Foreign Minister Kamal Thapa as telling a parliamentary committee.
The treaty requires both countries to treat each other's citizens as their own in matters of residence, property ownership, trade and commerce.
They are also committed in the treaty to inform each other of "any serious friction or misunderstanding" with neighbours.
Analysts say some provisions in the treaty are violated more often than they are honoured by either side.
Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral agreed on a visit to Nepal, a Himalayan kingdom, in June that foreign secretaries from the two countries should begin talks on the subject.
Thapa said Nepal, which is landlocked, was expected to start using a new land route to cross India to reach ports in Bangladesh from next month. This was approved by Gujral during his Nepal visit.
Mountainous Nepal has had access to the sea only through the Indian port of Calcutta, which accounts for 29 percent of the kingdom's total foreign trade.
Goods from Nepal will now be able to transit a small land corridor across northeastern India to reach Bangladesh.
Nepali businessmen using Calcutta port had complained of delays and congestions.
The new route connects Kakarvitta in Nepal with Banglaband in Bangladesh through a 71-km (44-mile) road across India which would cut transport costs and shipping delays for Nepal.
Thapa said "some progress" had been made with neighbouring Bhutan to repatriate some 100,000 refugees from Thimpu who have settled in camps in east Nepal. He did not elaborate.
Ethnic Nepalis began fleeing the Buddhist kingdom of Bhutan in 1990.

Bhutan authorities say arms dissidents of Nepali origin living in southern Bhutan instigated a revolt at that time against King Jigme Singye Wangchuck which coincided with a pro-democracy movement in Nepal.
The Nepalese government wants Bhutan to take back all refugees who hold documents proving their residence.
Bhutan says it cannot take back refugees who voluntarily left since under national laws they ceased to be Bhutanese citizens once they departed.
